doc.title: Phil Schaap interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Definition of the rhythm section
summary: Using Lawrence Lucie and Jo Jones, he assigns roles to bass, guitar, drums and piano.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Well obviously we’re going to have to do another part two or part three here. But I wanted to ask you about a couple of things, and one was your definition of the rhythm section?

Oh yeah. Jon Hendricks went crazy over that this morning here at the IAJE so I now realize that he wants me to put it down on paper, and to mail it to him. But you’re getting a thing. But this is really, you know I was raised by Jo Jones the drummer in the Basie band, and someone we haven’t mentioned yet which is Lawrence Lucie, the rhythm guitarist. He actually goes by Larry but he knows that everyone knows it’s Lawrence Lucie. He just turned 95. And most of this is Lawrence Lucie. It’s a little bit Jo Jones and a very little bit me, I’m sort of — but it’s got a stamp of approval from jazz people including this morning, Jo Jones. And one of the mysteries is why jazz had a rhythm guitarist. Rhythm sections were different in those days. Most people don’t understand it and couldn’t duplicate it not because musicians aren’t good. It’s cause there’s no way you’re going to be able to reprise that rhythm section concept with no understanding. So this is — and this is a little bit too harsh. I’m cutting things — it’s too concise, too pat, doesn’t leave enough room for the obvious exceptions that prove numerous other rules. This is the story. So you’ve got four guys. You’ve got piano, bass, guitar — acoustic guitar — and drums. Okay the bass. The bass player is in charge of four. Meaning he’s in charge of four four. The four four feel, that’s the bass player’s job. It’s got to be four four. The guitar player is in charge — it’s not in two four, but two four is always being played inside the four four. That’s the guitar player’s gig. The guitar player is in charge of two four, even though he’s playing in four four as well. But he’s in charge of not only the two four feel that’s within the four four feel, there’s sort of like two feels [scats] except I was doing more on one and three and that’s the difference. I was singing a bass player from the twenties instead of a rhythm guitarist in the thirties. The guitar player stings two and four but subtly.

It can’t be too bad, it has to be subtle, it has to be there. So the bass player is four, the guitar player is two four, the bass player is four four, the guitar player is two four, the guitar player is in charge of those unusual syncopation emphasises [sic] on two and four, okay? The drummer is in charge of swinging. He’s swinging. He better swing or he’s no good. Okay. The bass player and the piano — the bass player and the guitar player combined are in charge of making sure the drummer doesn’t rush, since he’s got to be so busy making sure it swings.
And the piano player is in charge of the music.
I’ll be darned. You know I’m going to have to think about this one.
And again, there are so many exceptions.
So what does a drummer do to make sure he’s swinging?
That’s up to the drummer. To try to sound like Jo Jones as best you can.
Okay. Well I’m glad we got that first, that’s cool.
